---
title: "Reading words in context"
subtitle: "Compare one word vector with one token occurrence vector"
description: "Learn how spaCy returns a context-sensitive token representation and why two occurrences of the same word can have different vectors."
categories: [similarity, contextual embeddings, spaCy]
---

A student underlines two occurrences of `bank` in a short text. The first names a
financial institution. The second names land beside a river.

The spelling is identical. The surrounding words make the two occurrences
different.

A **contextualized word representation** assigns a vector to each token
occurrence, an individual instance of a word or punctuation mark. A **word type**
groups occurrences with the same spelling. A contextual model can assign
different vectors to occurrences of the same word within a document.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- start the fixed local spaCy pipeline through the project helper
- confirm that the small pipeline has no static word-vector table
- read the token tensor produced for one text
- compare token occurrence vectors with an all-pair baseline
- examine same-sense controls
- separate contextual encoding from word-sense identification.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load the local spaCy pipeline

spaCy is a Python library. This project uses it through `R/use-spacy.R`. The
helper selects a fixed Python environment and prevents downloads during
rendering.

```{r}
library(reticulate)
library(spacyr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

source("R/use-spacy.R")

within_tolerance <- function(observed, expected, tolerance = 1e-3) {
  abs(observed - expected) < tolerance
}

pipeline <- use_project_spacy()
spacy_py <- import("spacy", delay_load = FALSE)
nlp <- spacy_py$load("en_core_web_sm")

pipeline_table <- tibble(
  item = c("pipeline", "static vector rows", "static vector columns"),
  value = c(
    pipeline$model,
    as.character(nlp$vocab$vectors$shape[[1]]),
    as.character(nlp$vocab$vectors$shape[[2]])
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  pipeline_table,
  col.names = c("Item", "Value"),
  caption = "The pinned small spaCy pipeline has no static word-vector table",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  pipeline$model == "en_core_web_sm",
  as.integer(nlp$vocab$vectors$shape[[1]]) == 0L,
  as.integer(nlp$vocab$vectors$shape[[2]]) == 0L
)
```

The zero-row vector table matters. This small pipeline does not store one
reusable vector for every word. It still produces an internal tensor, or array
of numbers, for the tokens it processes.

## Extract token occurrence vectors

A **tensor** is an array of numbers. For this text, spaCy returns one row per
token and 96 columns per token.

```{r}
text <- "The bank raised interest rates. He sat on the river bank and watched."
doc <- nlp(text)

tokens <- vapply(
  seq_len(length(doc)) - 1L,
  function(i) doc[i]$text,
  character(1)
)

tensor <- py_to_r(doc$tensor)

bank_positions <- which(tokens == "bank")
the_positions <- which(tokens %in% c("The", "the"))

token_table <- tibble(
  position = seq_along(tokens),
  token = tokens,
  target = case_when(
    position %in% bank_positions ~ "bank occurrence",
    position %in% the_positions ~ "the occurrence",
    TRUE ~ "other token"
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  token_table,
  col.names = c("Position", "Token", "Role in this lesson"),
  caption = "Tokens in the text and the positions compared below",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(tokens, c("The", "bank", "raised", "interest", "rates", ".", "He", "sat", "on", "the", "river", "bank", "and", "watched", ".")),
  identical(dim(tensor), c(15L, 96L)),
  identical(bank_positions, c(2L, 12L)),
  identical(the_positions, c(1L, 10L)),
  nrow(token_table) == 15L
)
```

The two `bank` tokens are at positions 2 and 12. They share spelling, but they do
not share the same tensor row.

## Compare occurrence vectors with a baseline

Cosine similarity compares vector direction. A score of 1 would mean the two rows
point in exactly the same direction. The two `bank` occurrence vectors score
about 0.3466.

```{r}
cosine <- function(first, second) {
  sum(first * second) / sqrt(sum(first^2) * sum(second^2))
}

all_pair_index <- which(
  upper.tri(matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(tokens), ncol = length(tokens))),
  arr.ind = TRUE
)

all_pair_cosines <- apply(
  all_pair_index,
  1,
  function(pair) cosine(tensor[pair[1], ], tensor[pair[2], ])
)

bank_cosine <- cosine(tensor[bank_positions[1], ], tensor[bank_positions[2], ])
the_cosine <- cosine(tensor[the_positions[1], ], tensor[the_positions[2], ])
bank_percentile <- mean(all_pair_cosines <= bank_cosine)
the_percentile <- mean(all_pair_cosines <= the_cosine)

all_pair_summary <- tibble(
  statistic = c("mean", "median", "5th percentile", "95th percentile"),
  cosine = c(
    mean(all_pair_cosines),
    median(all_pair_cosines),
    as.numeric(quantile(all_pair_cosines, 0.05)),
    as.numeric(quantile(all_pair_cosines, 0.95))
  )
)

comparison_table <- tibble(
  comparison = c("bank / bank", "the / the"),
  first_position = c(bank_positions[1], the_positions[1]),
  second_position = c(bank_positions[2], the_positions[2]),
  cosine_similarity = c(bank_cosine, the_cosine),
  percentile_of_all_pairs = c(bank_percentile, the_percentile)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  all_pair_summary |>
    mutate(cosine = round(cosine, 4)),
  col.names = c("All-pair baseline", "Cosine"),
  caption = "Cosine similarities across all 105 token pairs in the example text",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  comparison_table |>
    mutate(
      cosine_similarity = round(cosine_similarity, 4),
      percentile_of_all_pairs = round(percentile_of_all_pairs, 3)
    ),
  col.names = c("Comparison", "First position", "Second position", "Cosine similarity", "Percentile of all token pairs"),
  caption = "Repeated word strings compared with the all-pair baseline",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  length(all_pair_cosines) == 105L,
  within_tolerance(bank_cosine, 0.3466, tolerance = 1e-3),
  within_tolerance(the_cosine, 0.5322, tolerance = 1e-3),
  within_tolerance(mean(all_pair_cosines), 0.0476, tolerance = 1e-3),
  within_tolerance(median(all_pair_cosines), -0.0074, tolerance = 1e-3),
  within_tolerance(as.numeric(quantile(all_pair_cosines, 0.95)), 0.4475, tolerance = 1e-3),
  bank_percentile > 0.9,
  the_percentile > bank_percentile
)
```

The `bank` pair scores around the 91st percentile of the all-pair baseline for
the same text. The encoder assigns different vectors to individual occurrences.
The two `bank` rows remain closer than most token pairs in this short text.

## Examine same-sense controls

The stronger claim would be that the distance isolates word sense. The controls
below examine that claim through separate changes to sense and grammatical role.

```{r}
tensor_for_text <- function(text) {
  doc <- nlp(text)
  tokens <- vapply(
    seq_len(length(doc)) - 1L,
    function(i) doc[i]$text,
    character(1)
  )

  list(tokens = tokens, tensor = py_to_r(doc$tensor))
}

bank_pair_cosine <- function(text) {
  parsed <- tensor_for_text(text)
  positions <- which(parsed$tokens == "bank")

  if (length(positions) != 2L) {
    stop("Expected exactly two bank tokens.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  cosine(parsed$tensor[positions[1], ], parsed$tensor[positions[2], ])
}

bank_control_sentences <- tibble(
  comparison = c(
    "different senses, different roles",
    "same financial sense, same role",
    "same river sense",
    "same financial sense, different roles"
  ),
  text = c(
    "The bank raised interest rates. He sat on the river bank and watched.",
    "The bank raised interest rates. The bank approved the loan.",
    "He sat on the river bank and watched. She walked along the muddy bank.",
    "The bank approved the loan. She walked into the bank."
  ),
  cosine_similarity = c(
    bank_pair_cosine(text[1]),
    bank_pair_cosine(text[2]),
    bank_pair_cosine(text[3]),
    bank_pair_cosine(text[4])
  )
)

role_gap <- abs(
  bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity[bank_control_sentences$comparison == "different senses, different roles"] -
    bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity[bank_control_sentences$comparison == "same financial sense, different roles"]
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  bank_control_sentences |>
    mutate(cosine_similarity = round(cosine_similarity, 4)),
  col.names = c("Comparison", "Sentences", "Cosine similarity"),
  caption = "Same-sense controls for two occurrences of bank",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(bank_control_sentences) == 4L,
  all(within_tolerance(
    bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity,
    c(0.3466, 0.9422, 0.5900, 0.3447),
    tolerance = 1e-3
  )),
  role_gap < 0.01,
  bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity[2] > 0.9,
  bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity[2] > bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity[1]
)
```

The same financial sense in different grammatical roles scores about 0.3447.
Different senses in different roles score almost the same, about 0.3466. The same
financial sense in the same role scores about 0.9422. In these
four examples, the grammatical-role contrast is at least as large as the
dictionary-sense contrast. These examples illustrate the representation, not a
word-sense evaluation. There is no benchmark or independent sense labeling here.

## Contrast with one vector per word

The word2vec lesson uses a saved model with one trained vector for each retained
word type. A
one-vector-per-word model cannot give river `bank` and finance `bank` two rows in
the same sentence. A contextual pipeline can.

Different vectors do not show that the model finds the intended dictionary sense.
The `en_core_web_sm` tok2vec layer, short for token-to-vector, converts each token
into numbers. The tagger, parser, and named-entity recognizer use this shared
encoder. Training targets those tasks, not word-sense identification.

A representation can change with context without finding the intended word
sense. This encoder belongs to a small pipeline, not a large language model.

```{r}
final_checks <- tibble(
  check = c("token rows", "tensor dimensions", "bank cosine rounded", "same-role financial cosine rounded", "static vector rows"),
  value = c(
    as.character(nrow(tensor)),
    paste(ncol(tensor), "columns"),
    sprintf("%.4f", bank_cosine),
    sprintf("%.4f", bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity[2]),
    as.character(nlp$vocab$vectors$shape[[1]])
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  final_checks,
  col.names = c("Check", "Value"),
  caption = "Final checks for the contextual representation example",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(tensor) == 15L,
  ncol(tensor) == 96L,
  within_tolerance(bank_cosine, 0.3466, tolerance = 1e-3),
  within_tolerance(bank_control_sentences$cosine_similarity[2], 0.9422, tolerance = 1e-3),
  as.integer(nlp$vocab$vectors$shape[[1]]) == 0L,
  identical(tokens[bank_positions], c("bank", "bank")),
  identical(tokens[the_positions], c("The", "the"))
)
```

## What to remember

- A contextualized representation gives one vector to each token occurrence.
- The pinned small spaCy pipeline has 0 rows in its static vector table.
- The example text produces a 15 by 96 tensor.
- The two `bank` occurrence vectors score about 0.3466, above most token pairs in
  that text.
- In these four examples, grammatical role matters at least as much as the
  dictionary-sense contrast. These examples are not a word-sense benchmark.
